en: Preface to the *Commentary on the Opening of the Doctrinal Tenets of the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna*.
Now, as for the phrase "The All-Knowing One" (*sarvajña*): his comprehensive illumination unifies the ultimate and the conventional within the source of the mind;

his profound compassion universally permeates, unfolding the teachings of both the Half- and Full-Wheel [Dharmacakras] through the branches of his speech. The word "now" (*fu*) serves as the opening of the discourse. As for "opening" (*xu*), it refers to...
The collective silk emerging from the mouths of silkworms is called "threads" (*xu*).
This is because the collective arises from the collective;
furthermore, "collective" carries the meaning of "head-threads" (*tóuxù*).
It is capable of producing cloth sufficient to ward off cold and heat, thereby fulfilling the wishes of people.
As for the term "omniscient" (sarvajña):
it means that ordinary worldlings, being deluded and ignorant, are entirely termed "non-knowing."
Although the practitioners of the two vehicles know [this], their knowledge has limits;
the wisdom they arouse is not all-pervasive, and thus they do not attain universal knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) transcend these two preceding categories.
Although those in the mundane and supramundane realms possess knowledge,
because they still possess subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
they cannot be called "Omniscient" (*sarvajña*) like the Buddha.
"Only the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, universally know all the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings throughout the three realms and six destinies;
this is called 'universal knowledge,' and so forth. As for the term "thoroughly illuminating":
"委" (wei) means "minute" or "detailed.
"Zhào" (zhào) arises from "illumination" (míng).
The wisdom of the two vehicles can illuminate the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
Ordinary beings, through their deluded attachments, cling to all things as existent;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having realized the emptiness of persons and phenomena,
fully comprehend both the ultimate and conventional truths.
Regarding the statement that "one can thoroughly illuminate both the mundane and the supramundane, blending the ultimate and the conventional within the source of the mind":
"blending" (*hun*) means intermingling and harmonizing.
This refers to the harmonious integration of the dharmas of the ultimate and the conventional within the single source of the mind.
The source of the single mind can contain all phenomena;
it is for this reason that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to extend their profound compassion universally.
"Qia" (洽) means "moistening and nourishing," and so forth. Regarding the term "profound compassion":
all sentient beings are completely submerged in extreme attachments;
the Buddha, by means of right wisdom, transcends [these] through great compassion.
Universally transporting those in the three realms to transcend both existence and non-existence—
truly, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa;
such is the profundity of this compassion that is free from marks.
There are two kinds of compassion based on the perception of signs:
that which arises from the conjunction of craving and views belongs to those with adventitious afflictions;
that which is produced by relying on meditative concentration belongs to those of the Two Vehicles.
Great compassion without conditions is free from the marks of self and other;
within the equal dharma-realm, ordinary beings and sages are identical.
How could one perceive a distinction between self and other within this single suchness?
Ordinary beings and sages alike realize that compassion possesses three types.
When ordinary beings give rise to compassion only after first conceiving the notion of a self,
it is called "compassion with a self as its object" (ātmālambana-maitrī).
One gives rise to compassion for one's own friends and kinsmen.
Those of the Two Vehicles see that sentient beings are constantly oppressed by the convergence of the three sufferings, the five sufferings, and the eight sufferings.
To deliver others through the Dharma and perceive those who may be delivered is called "compassion conditioned by the Dharma.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have attained the wisdom of equality.
Awakening to the compassion of the same essence, one contemplates all sentient beings as having the aspect of one’s own children;
being perfectly equal and impartial toward both enemies and kin, and so forth. As for the statement, "expounding the provisional and the ultimate through the branching of words":
For example, when children of the world first go to school,
they first learn characters such as "shang" (上) and "dafu" (大夫),
which are called "half-letters"; later, by combining many such characters, they form a single complete word.
He causes the assembly of consciousness to reach completion through full syllables.
Initially, for those of shallow faculties,
he teaches the Small Vehicle doctrines such as the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
The *Anupravartana-yukti-mukha* speaks only of the six consciousnesses;
this is called the teaching of "half-syllables.
Later, for the sake of those bodhisattvas whose faculties of faith are profound and mature...
To expound the Mahāyāna of definitive meaning and establish the teaching of the Middle Way of the eight consciousnesses is called the "full-syllable" (pūrṇākṣara).
"Schools (pāda) mean branches and extensions," and so forth.

Indeed, it is because of nature and characteristics that all phenomena are further integrated and returned to the single suchness; thus, the meanings of the texts mutually fuse, and the eight collections of scripture flow through the four analytical eloquences. Regarding the phrase "Indeed, it is because of nature and characteristics that they are further integrated," etc.: [the explanation follows].
"Shi" means reality.
For those who are ignorant and deluded, essence and characteristics appear to be divergent paths;
for those who achieve harmonious integration, however, all phenomena converge upon a single track.
If we discuss the nature, it is not separate from its characteristics;
if we discuss the characteristics, they are not separate from their nature.
It is also like raising waves that are not separate from water.
Raising water does not separate it from its waves;
water and waves share the same source and are fundamentally no different in their moisture.
Thus, the myriad dharmas all return to the single suchness, and so forth. Furthermore, because the substance of the various natures is fundamentally not different.
All arise from the veiling of True Suchness by views and appearances;
milk, curd, and clarified butter are originally of one flavor.
Failing to understand the beginning and the end, one perceives only their differences.
Regarding the statement that "text and meaning are mutually integrated," "text" refers to names, phrases, and phonemes;
"meaning" refers to the principles elucidated by them. As for the "eight treasuries" (aṣṭapiṭaka):
The Sūtras, Vinaya, Abhidharma, and the Miscellaneous Piṭaka (Kṣudraka-piṭaka), etc.,
constitute the four piṭakas for each of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Regarding the phrase "the words gallop," "galloping" means to rush or hasten toward.
Like a bird soaring swiftly through the void,
he now gallops with the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*) to elucidate and expound their meaning;
by means of these four analytical knowledges, he gallops across the surging waves.
"The depth and shallowness of the textual meaning are proclaimed and expounded by means of the oceanic mouth," and so forth. Regarding the "four analytical knowledges" (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ):
at the time of preaching the Dharma, one is unimpeded regarding the sounds of speech, the phrasing, and the principles of the doctrine.
The unimpeded eloquence of names and phrases:
the teachings and principles he expounds follow one another in sequence, remaining inexhaustible throughout vast eons.
This is the unimpeded eloquence of names and meanings.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, establish teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings;
they explain both nature and characteristics without any doubt or obstruction.
This is called the unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
The words and meanings spoken by the Tathāgata are manifold.
He expounds with a single voice, yet each according to their kind attains understanding.
With skillful means and abundant wisdom, he is ever without weariness.
The words and principles employed are free from any impediment or difficulty;
this is called "eloquent exposition.
The Dharma taught is likewise free from any obstruction or stagnation.
"Regarding the phrase 'the eyes are unimpeded,' and so forth:
what is the difference between emptiness and existence? Why do the paths diverge in their breadth and brevity? To illustrate this, ten thousand records follow a single track. What does 'what' mean?"
The term "tracks" refers to the paths of travel.
The designations of "emptiness" and "existence" are intentional, provisional teachings.
When this is investigated to its ultimate conclusion, emptiness and existence are not different.
Existence is the substantiality of the aggregates as grasped by views;
emptiness is their conventional formation, realized as being non-existent in essence.
It is clearly understood that delusion and awakening are distinct in their origins, yet their fundamental nature is such that existence and emptiness are not different.
The words of the extensive and the concise are in truth not two.
If one awakens, the four lines are sufficient and there is no need for further seeking; this is the concise approach.
If one is deluded, even if one reads ten thousand scrolls of true words, it is of no avail.
This is essentially the same as the extensive version of the *Zhengwang* (Falling into Delusion).
However, while there are differences in the sharpness or dullness [of faculties], there is no duality between the extensive and the abbreviated versions. Why is this so? And so forth.

Those who investigate the root will surely find the same flavor in the hundred rivers; those who stagnate at the branches compete in the turbulent flow of the five slanders. Regarding the phrase "investigating the root":
"investigate" (jiu) means to exhaustively pursue (qiong).
The "Fundamental" (ben) refers to the essence (ti).
It is the state where names are extinguished and marks are severed;
it is ultimate truth.
To speak in terms of comprehensive integration:
if one fundamentally attains the source,
one will know that all streams converge into the same ocean.
By tasting a drop of water from the great ocean,
one knows the flavor of all its currents. When speech lags at the branches,
such lagging arises from delusion.
The term "extremists" (*anta*) refers to those who cling to emptiness while still possessing the teachings;
this is discussed in terms of their biased attachments.
As the *Dvādaśanikāya-sūtra* states:
On a certain night I attained perfect enlightenment, and on a certain night I entered parinirvāṇa.
Between these two moments,
I have not spoken a single word.
To say that this was not spoken by the Buddha, or to claim that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma,
is to slander the Buddha;
such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
One clearly knows that the Dharma of the fundamental substance transcends the reach of verbal expression;
this mind wishes to contemplate it, yet deliberation vanishes.
The mouth desires to speak, yet the words fail;
it cannot be known through intellectual understanding,
nor can it be recognized through conscious awareness.
There are those of biased views who immediately establish these five types of slander.
Furthermore, the names of the five slanders are as follows:
first, the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*).
Second, the denial of diminution;
third, the denial of contradiction;
fourth, the denial of conceptual proliferation.
The five delusions lead to abandonment and slander.
To explain each of these five slanders individually:
first, one says that all phenomena exist.
Dharmas are fundamentally non-existent;
to say they exist is the slander of superimposition.
The nature of dharmas is fundamentally empty.
How can it be said that [things] exist?
Second, although it is said that all dharmas are non-existent,
the fundamental dharma is not non-existent.
To say "it does not exist" is a deprecatory denial (*apavāda*).
Since the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists,
how can one say it does not exist?
The third is both existence and non-existence.
This fundamental dharma is free from both existence and non-existence;
[to claim otherwise] is a contradictory denial.
To assert both emptiness and existence simultaneously would contradict the principle.
Fourth, it is neither existent nor non-existent;
this fundamental dharma has no coming and is not existent.
To say that it does not exist even now is the slander of conceptual proliferation;
to say that what is not existent is empty [is likewise].
To claim that what is non-existent exists is not the case;
since emptiness and existence are indeterminate,
one clearly understands this to be mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
If one were to establish even a single dharma as a conceptual designation (*nāma-rūpa*),
it would all become mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
The five [aggregates] are neither existent nor non-existent.
The fundamental Dharma has no written characters or spoken language.
If one says that the Dharma has no name, [it is because it transcends such designations].
This is the deluded slander.
Reversing the fourth [position] establishes the fifth:
the statement that "what is not empty is existent."
That which exists is not [ultimately] existent;
what is called "non-existent" is emptiness.
That which does not exist is not [ultimately] non-existent.
That which exists is not existence;
it thus results in the meaning of non-existence.
That which does not exist is not non-existence.
This, however, results in a contradiction. If this were the case,
it would be clear that those who are deluded and ignorant are not truly wise.

Therefore, the Hinayana drifts in the ocean of existence, while the various tenets of the Sarvastivadins flourish; the ultimate truth is submerged in emptiness, and contentious debates arise in profusion. Regarding the statement, "Therefore, the Hinayana drifts in the ocean of existence": [the explanation follows].
"Drifting" means floating.
Since both the self of persons and the self of phenomena are definitively existent, it is said that there are "two existences.
As for the statement, "those who are submerged in the emptiness of emptiness regarding the ultimate truth," it refers to those who are lost in a mere void.
"To drown" means to sink.
Since both of the aforementioned meanings are entirely empty,
they are called the "two emptinesses."
The former school clings to existence,
while the latter stagnates in emptiness;
as emptiness and existence are mutually contradictory, contentious debates arise in competition.
Regarding the "person-self" (*pudgala-ātman*):
it refers to the arbitrary conceptualization of a person existing at the locus where the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are provisionally combined.
Apart from "self" and "what belongs to self," there is no person-self; this is "person-non-self" (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Regarding the term "dharma-ātman" (self of phenomena):
it refers to the attachment to causally conditioned phenomena as being truly produced and arising with an intrinsic nature;
therefore, they are called "self."
All phenomena arising through causes and conditions are entirely illusory;
fundamentally unborn, their essence is without movement.
There is no self in phenomena.

"Still driving away delusive objects, one has not yet transcended the dark thoroughfare; in vain one turns toward the true breeze and fruitlessly receives the Dharma rain. Regarding the phrase "still driving away delusive objects":

sinking into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or dwelling in existence (*bhava*) is collectively termed "delusive objects. Regarding "not yet transcending the dark thoroughfare": [this refers to remaining within the realm of ignorance].
It is a path of darkness.
If one gives rise to such deviant views, one has not yet transcended the cycle of saṃsāra;
those who merely claim to be heading toward the true wind [of the Dharma] are in vain.
Those who cling to partiality labor in vain as they pursue the True Teaching;
"wind" signifies transformation, like wind bending the grass.
Those who turn their backs on the vision are like withered trees.
"The method of dew and moisture is like rain," and so forth.

Therefore, I, Maitreya, the one in the position of succession, extensively expound the Yoga [Śāstra], closing the gates of dualistic views and opening the path of the single reality. Regarding the phrase "Maitreya, the one in the position of succession": [text continues].
Just as a worldly king appoints his crown prince in advance to succeed him in the administration of the state,
so that when the king passes away, the prince immediately succeeds him as the sovereign;
even so is it with those who are bodhisattvas in their final birth.
The Buddha gave him this prediction:
"In the future, when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years,
during the time of the Cakravartin King Rāgha, you shall become a Buddha as his successor."
In the Sanskrit language, it is called Maitreya;
this is abbreviated as Mili.
Mili is his clan name.
This is translated as "Maitreya.
"Ajita" is his name;
here it means "Unconquerable."
No one surpasses him;
therefore, this Bodhisattva is named Ajita (Invincible).
As for Maitreya:
Because this bodhisattva possesses profound compassion,
their earnest resolve to rescue those in suffering is called "loving-kindness" (maitrī).
The limited loving-kindness of the two vehicles observes only the desire realm.

The Great Compassion of the Buddha universally delivers those within the three realms. "Chǎn" (闡) means to expound or to propagate; "dù" (杜) means to block or to obstruct. The "two gates of views" refers to the gates of emptiness and existence. "Opening the single path of reality" refers to the Middle Way. However, because principle encompasses all things and the breadth of the teachings causes the intent to disperse across words, former practitioners grew weary of transmitting them, and later students grew exhausted in their pursuit of study. As for the phrase "however, because... [it serves to introduce this difficulty].
However, it is by virtue of arising;
it is by virtue of being common. "Comprehensive" (*gai*) means to encompass; it is also to include.
To spread horizontally is called "comprehensive. "Extensive" (*baku*) means to penetrate. "Profound" (*shii*) means intention. "Vast" (*kō*) means great.

On the twelfth day of the twelfth month of the Xin-you year, there was a bodhisattva whose name was Vasubandhu. His rank reached the pinnacle of the Three Sages, and his virtue bordered upon that of the Ten Holy Ones. He composed a thousand treatises, his fame resounded throughout the Five Indias, he perfectly accorded with the Buddha’s mind, and he elegantly supported the prophetic records. *Yuan* (爰) means "at" or "in. *Jue* (厥) means "his" or "that. Regarding "his rank reached the pinnacle of the Three Sages": this refers to the three stages of the Path of Training (*śaikṣa-mārga*). Specifically, it denotes that he had attained the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and was approaching the stage of Arhatship (*arhat*). The "Three Sages" are the fruits of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and Non-returner; since he had already realized the fruit of Non-returner, his status was thus described as reaching the "pinnacle" of these three. Furthermore, the "Three Sages" may also refer to the three types of Arhats: those liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*), those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), and those who have attained mastery over their faculties (*indriya-vaśitā-prāpta*). Because he had attained the fruit of Non-returner, he was capable of attaining Arhatship at will; therefore, he is said to have reached the "pinnacle" of these three sages. As for "virtue bordering on the Ten Holy Ones," the "Ten Holy Ones" refers to the ten stages of the Bodhisattva path. Since he had not yet entered the Bodhisattva grounds (*bhūmi*), his virtue was said to be "bordering" upon them. It is also possible that the term "Ten Holy Ones" here refers to the ten types of Arhats. Because he had attained the fruit of Non-returner, he was capable of attaining Arhatship at will; therefore, his virtue was said to be "bordering" upon the Ten Holy Ones. Regarding "he composed a thousand treatises": this refers to the fact that he authored approximately one thousand works, such as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the *Vyākhyāyukti*, the *Karma-siddhi-prakaraṇa*, the *Vijñapti-mātratā-siddhi-śāstra*, and others. Regarding "his fame resounded throughout the Five Indias": this means that his reputation spread throughout the five regions of India—namely, the eastern, western, southern, northern, and central regions. Regarding "perfectly accords with the Buddha’s mind": this means that his teachings were in complete harmony with the intent of the Tathāgata. Regarding "elegantly supports the prophetic records": this refers to the fact that his doctrines accorded with the predictions found in the scriptures. For example, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states: "In the future, after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Vasubandhu. He will compose a treatise called the *Kośa*. This treatise will be like a great ocean, containing all the profound meanings of the Dharma. It will be able to refute the heterodox views of the various schools and establish the true principles of the Mahāyāna. It will be able to benefit sentient beings and cause them to attain liberation. Because his teachings accorded with such prophecies, they are said to "elegantly support" them. Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "After my parinirvāṇa, in the future age, there will be a bhikṣu named Vasubandhu. He will compose a treatise called the *Kośa*. This treatise will be like a great ocean, containing all the profound meanings of the Dharma. It will be able to refute the heterodox views of the various schools and establish the true principles of the Mahāyāna. It will be able to benefit sentient beings and cause them to attain liberation. Because his teachings accord with such prophecies, they are said to "elegantly support" them. Moreover, the *Buddhabhāṣita-sarvabuddha-viṣayāvatāra-jñānālokālaṃkāra-sūtra* states: "In the future, after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Vasubandhu. He will compose a treatise called the *Kośa*. This treatise will be like a great ocean, containing all the profound meanings of the Dharma. It will be able to refute the heterodox views of the various schools and establish the true principles of the Mahāyāna. It will be able to benefit sentient beings and cause them to attain liberation. Because his teachings accord with such prophecies, they are said to "elegantly support" them. Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "In the future, after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Vasubandhu. He will compose a treatise called the *Kośa*. This treatise will be like a great ocean, containing all the profound meanings of the Dharma. It will be able to refute the heterodox views of the various schools and establish the true principles of the Mahāyāna. It will be able to benefit sentient beings and cause them to attain liberation. Because his teachings accord with such prophecies, they are said to "elegantly support" them. This treatise will be like a great ocean, containing all the profound meanings of the Dharma. This treatise will be like a great ocean, containing all the profound meanings of the Dharma. It will be able to refute the heterodox views of the various schools and establish the true principles of the Mahāyāna
This Bodhisattva was a close friend of the worldly devas;
he was called Vasubandhu, also known as Devabandhu,
and resided among the three stages of worthiness prior to the ten stages of the bodhisattva path.
This refers to a person in the subsequent stage of application (*prāyogika*).
"Ultimate" (*parama*) means "venerable.
As for the "worthy one" (*bhadra*), their conceptual mind is slightly diminished.
One who practices goodness and is well-disciplined is called "virtuous" (*xian*).

Furthermore, one whose conduct is truly harmonious and upright is called "virtuous. To say that their virtue is "neighboring the ten sages" means that their virtuous deeds approximate those of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
It is not entering the true stage (*bhūmi*).
As for "stage," it is that which is able to generate and bring forth the Buddha-wisdom.
Second, the metaphor of "arising great compassion of the same essence" refers to bearing the burden of all beings.
As for the term "sage" (ārya):
because they accord with principle, penetrate the divine, and possess unimpeded skillful means and transformations, they are called sages.
It is said that although the three types of worthy persons (trīṇi kalyāṇapudgalāni) realize the true doctrine,
their habitual obstructions have not yet been eliminated and their taints and delusions still persist; therefore, they are called "inner ordinary persons" (adhyātma-prthagjana).
To summarize the initial stage of the ten faiths:
throughout all thirty minds, one practices the contemplation of emptiness and non-self.
To discuss them specifically:
In the first ten stages (bhūmi), one cultivates the contemplation of the selflessness of persons;
in the next ten practices (caryā), one cultivates the contemplation of the selflessness of dharmas through dependent origination;
and in the subsequent ten dedications (pariṇāmanā), one cultivates the contemplation of the selflessness of dharmas through suchness (tathatā).
Next, on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one practices the contemplation of the three emptinesses and the two kinds of selflessness.

Next, at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one practices the contemplation of illumination-and-quiescence; if one has already realized [emptiness], one performs only the contemplation of quiescence.
He contemplates the great tranquility of the Buddha-ground of equality.
This noble master composed five hundred treatises each for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles;
thus, he is renowned in the West as the "Master of a Thousand Treatises. As for the Five Indias: [text continues]
This is called "Heaven. "Qi" (契) means meeting or harmonizing. "Ya" (雅) means wondrous.
"Xuánjì" (懸記) refers to the Buddha’s prophecy that this person shall be the twenty-second successor in the transmission of the Dharma after my parinirvāṇa.
"If it is indeed as this prediction states, it would truly accord with the Sage’s heart," he said.

Thus, he was moved by compassion for those of his time whose faculties were meager and whose natures shallow; they feared the ocean of the Dharma and remained long estranged from it, and were intimidated by the mountain of its meaning, forever discouraged. "Moved" refers to his compassionate concern. They feared the great origins of the Abhidharma-kośa Śāstra as much as they feared the ocean.
A heart of estrangement and separation arises;
"separation" (kui) means being apart or distinct. The profound principles of the *Kie-ka-lun* (Kāśyapaparivarta) are like a mountain in appearance—truly difficult to cross.

A sense of discouragement and alienation arose, whereupon he extracted the essence from the extensive scriptures and condensed the fundamental tenets into this brief text. To guide those of initial capacity, he compiled this minor treatise. As for what is meant by "extracting": [The remainder of the passage follows.]
"Shi" (拾) means to gather; it carries the sense of gathering and picking up.

"Guangbu" (廣部) refers to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. "Wan" (綰) means to grasp or encompass. "You" (誘) means to lead or guide. "Ji" (機) refers to the faculties or roots (*indriya*). "Zuan" (纂) means to compile or collect. "Xiaolun" (小論) refers to the *Śata-dharma-vidyā-mukha-śāstra* (Treatise on the One Hundred Dharmas).

Desiring to cause them to linger in the ultimate teaching so they might gradually be imbued with the True Vehicle, [the author] shows that weakness leads to the loss of one's direction of return, thereby leading exhausted followers onto a shortcut. Regarding "lingering in the ultimate teaching":
"liu-lian" means to remain attached to or to linger in.
Because the Mahāyāna sūtras are integrated, they do not sink into insignificance; thus,
one awakens to the Great through the Small,
and traverses the Deep by means of the Shallow.

To cause the Great Dharma to remain for a long time, to be inherited and flourish without interruption—this is called "continuous preservation" (*liánliú*). To be gradually permeated by the True Vehicle refers to "habitual cultivation.
Gradual study is easily accomplished;
sudden permeation is difficult to achieve.
It is like the worldly reception of form:
through habitual practice, one becomes a sage; gradually being permeated, one attains the truth.
As the common saying goes:
Those who associate with the vermilion become vermilion;
those who associate with the ink become ink-colored;
those who associate with the sycophant become sycophantic.
The virtue of associating with the worthy causes those who have strayed in their youth to return to the Vaipulya.
"Those who have strayed in their youth" are like young children who, having lost their parents, are disoriented regarding their dwelling place;
they must rely on a wise person to show them the way, just as one does for a small child.
This metaphor refers to deluded sentient beings.
"Returning to the proper direction" is a metaphor for the ultimate teaching.
"Guiding the weary travelers" refers to those with deviant views—the followers of the Two Vehicles who are confused regarding the Great Teaching.
Having mistakenly entered onto deviant paths, one undergoes all manner of hardships and toil.
The Sage rebukes such backsliding, fearing that it will lead to a severance of one's spiritual affinity; the path is so remote that it is difficult to ascend.
Therefore, he reveals the direct route.
This is precisely this treatise.

It first clarifies the existence of the hundred dharmas and subsequently reveals the emptiness of the two selves; thus, the beginning and end illuminate one another, and the commencement and conclusion reflect each other. Regarding "first clarifying the existence of the hundred dharmas":
The principles of the dependent and the perfected natures are established through mutual causality;
they arise by way of mutual reliance.
The essence of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is fundamentally suchness;
its constant nature is unchanging.
This reveals the existence of the two [natures]. Next, the revelation of the two emptinesses:
The dual attachments to persons and phenomena are the deluded mind of conceptualization;
they are merely false sentiments and vain imaginings.
If the delusion of perception ceases, persons and phenomena are fundamentally empty.

This reveals that fundamentally there is no grasping at a self. "Beginning" refers to the initial stage; "end" refers to the final stage. Regarding the term "mutually illuminating," "illuminating" (huī) means clarity.
The preceding text explained that conditioned phenomena exist in order to dispel the attachment to emptiness.
The teaching that emptiness is explained at the end is for the purpose of eliminating the view of existence. As for "the beginning and the end reflecting one another":
taking the former to reflect the latter, it is empty yet not non-empty;
taking the latter to reflect the former, it exists yet not as a substantial existence.
Having clearly realized that things are neither empty nor existent, they are discarded. Once biased attachments are discarded, the discarding itself is eliminated.

When attachment to extremes is eliminated, the Middle Way (madhyamaka) begins to manifest; thus, the waves of consciousness subside and fade away, and the true source becomes clear and vast by virtue of this. To speak of the "Middle Way" (madhyamaka) is to refer to the Middle Path. "Begins to manifest" (zhào) means the initial emergence. "Manifests" (zhāng) means to clarify. As for "waves of consciousness," it refers to the surging movements of the mind.

The consciousness-mind is like waves; "obscured" (*yin*) means submerged; "subtle" (*wei*) means weak; "true source" (*zhenyuan*) refers to one's original nature; "relying" (*lai*) means depending upon; "clear" (*cheng*) means pure; and "vast" (*kuo*) means limpid.
When the waves subside, the sea becomes clear;
when delusion is removed, the nature becomes vast. One is the beginning of numbers;
ten is the end of numbers.
Together they become scholars.
A scholar must maintain integrity from beginning to end;
such a person is called a superior scholar (upapudgala).
"Exquisite indeed is the profound significance of this treatise! "Exquisite" (*zhì*) means great; "profound" (*yōu*) means deep; "significance" (*qù*) means intention or orientation.

The title at the beginning, *Mahāyāna-śatadharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra*, cites the superior benefit of what is followed as the general name for its own school. Regarding "citing the superior benefit of what is followed": [it refers to the fact that]...

This treatise takes the Mahāyāna as its primary tenet; thus it is called "the tenet. To bring benefit to all classes of beings by means of this vehicle is called "supreme benefit. "Established" (kṛta) means "founded" (sthāpita). Regarding the general name of one's own school:
Within the Mahāyāna, it is called the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*.

Furthermore, the phrase "a brief record of names and numbers from the *Mūla-vastu*" indicates the unique basis for the arising of this treatise and distinguishes its specific title from other expositions. Regarding "indicating the unique basis for the arising of the treatise": [The text continues with the explanation of the title.]
This treatise is certainly derived from the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section) of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and not from any other sections of the *Abhidharma*.
This is to distinguish it from other specific titles used for its exposition.
Although this treatise is derived from the *Maulī-bhūmi* (Basic Section),
it is established under a distinct title as the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas),
rather than being referred to simply as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Nor is it titled the *Mūlaprakaraṇa-śāstra*.
In the Mahāyāna, the name is established by manifesting the essence and enumeration through the exalted title "One Hundred Dharmas.
"Mahā" (Great) is named by excluding the Small [Vehicle]. "Yāna" (Vehicle) has the meaning of "transporting" or "carrying across."
The designation is also established through apophatic definition (*paryudāsa*).
Apophatic definition means that it distinguishes [this teaching] from the Lesser Vehicle; it is not a cataphatic definition (*vidhi*). "Hundred" (*śata*) refers to number;
ten tens supporting one another is called a hundred. "Dharma" refers to the essence (*tattva*).
Speaking in terms of its essential substance, one hundred items are established and determined. "Enlightenment" (*ming*) refers to wisdom; "gate" (*men*) refers to penetration.
These one hundred dharmas are the gates through which wisdom travels;
they are taken as the merit because they alone can open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. As for "treatise" (*lun*): [it is that which analyzes and establishes these matters].
The Treatise on Discerning Right Principle and Distinguishing the Profound from the False is titled *Lun*. As for "original substance" (*ben shi*), it refers to the fundamental essence;
it is the essence of the hundred dharmas. "Investigate" (*jiu*) means to exhaustively penetrate; "ultimate" (*ji*) means wondrous.
"Within the sections" refers to the topical categories of this specific portion.
As for the phrase "within the sections," it means within the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section), and not within the other sections.

"An abridged record" means to suppress those verbose words and numerical categories while raising these essential outlines. "Abridged" refers to omitting redundant and cumbersome expressions; "recorded" refers to documenting the essential outlines and profound principles. "To suppress" means to reach the ultimate [truth].

To manifest refined inclinations and establish a grand title, I have thus briefly recorded the names and numbers from the "Section on the Fundamental Matter" within the *Mahāyāna-śata-dharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra*. "Jing" (旌) means to signify; it refers to a banner.
Now, by raising a banner one comes to know military strategy; by using a firm emblem one’s authenticity is made manifest.
If one wishes to discern the strength of an army, one need only observe its banners and flags.
If one wishes to know this Dharma, which is exceedingly profound, one should examine the titles used to express it: *ya* (雅) means correct and subtle; *hong* (鴻) means great.
The exposition was completed on the fourteenth day; it was finished on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month in the year of Xinyou.
From the preface... [text missing].
